title: 我为一款 EEG 可穿戴设备注册了设计。然后我测试了电极是否放在正确的位置。
author: Bhumii Shah
content:
I hold a UK registered design (6521594) for a wearable that looks for early signs of Alzheimer’s disease. It is a wraparound visor. Dry EEG electrodes sit at the temples and forehead. An infrared eye-tracking sensor sits in the front lens panel.

The placement was chosen for wearability. Wet gel electrodes give a better signal, but they are messy and slow, and nobody is going to put conductive gel on their scalp every morning. A visor with dry contacts goes on like glasses. For a device meant to track change over months rather than capture one clinical snapshot, being worn consistently matters more than perfect signal in any single session.

That was the reasoning. I still think it is right.

But it left a question I had been avoiding.

The problem with the placement

The most reliable EEG marker for Alzheimer’s is slowing of the posterior alpha rhythm — reduced alpha power at the back of the head, over parietal and occipital regions. That is where the literature consistently points.

My device cannot reach those sites. A wraparound visor sits at the front and sides. The back of the frame holds the processing unit, for weight balance. There are no electrodes there and there were never going to be.

So the device is built to detect a condition using a signal it is positioned away from. Either frontal-temporal channels carry enough on their own, or the form factor is wrong. Finding that out after building hardware would be expensive.

I had been treating it as something to resolve later. Then I realised I already had the data to answer it.

The dataset makes it testable

OpenNeuro ds004504 is 88 subjects of 19-channel clinical EEG — Alzheimer’s, frontotemporal dementia, healthy controls. Resting state, eyes closed.

I already had a pipeline on it. Welch PSD, relative power in delta, theta, alpha and beta, plus theta/alpha and delta/beta ratios. One feature vector per subject. Random Forest, evaluated leave-one-subject-out.

Nineteen channels means I can subset them. Take only the electrodes my visor would have, run the same pipeline, compare against the full montage.

Three conditions: 


REGIONS = { 
# Approximates the device: forehead and temples. 
    "device-like": [ 
      "Fp1", "Fp2", "F3", "F4", "F7", "F8", "Fz", # forehead 
        "T3", "T4", "T7", "T8", # temples 
    ], 
    # Where the literature reports the strongest signal. 
    "posterior": [ 
        "P3", "P4", "Pz", "O1", "O2",
        "T5", "T6", "P7", "P8", 
    ], 
    # Baseline - every channel. 
    "whole-head": None, 
}

Both naming conventions are listed. Older recordings use T3/T4/T5/T6, newer ones use T7/T8/P7/P8 for the same physical positions. Unmatched names are ignored, so the script runs either way. In ds004504 that resolves to 9 device-like channels and 7 posterior.

The feature extraction mirrors the main pipeline exactly. Same Welch parameters, same bands, same ratios, same classifier, same evaluation. The only thing that changes between conditions is which electrodes are included. If the feature definitions differed too, the comparison would mean nothing.

Setting the threshold before the run

The interpretation was written into the script before it ran, not after the numbers came back:

If device-like performs close to whole-head, the sensor placement is supported by evidence rather than assumption.

If device-like performs clearly worse, that is an important finding before any hardware is built — and it belongs in the roadmap, not hidden.

The threshold was fixed at the same time. With roughly 65 subjects, differences under about 0.05 ROC-AUC are noise.

I had a stake in one outcome. I have a registered design and I wanted the frontal-temporal channels to work. If the numbers had come first and the threshold second, I would have found a way to read almost any result as validation. Not dishonestly. Just the ordinary thing where you build a reasonable story after you already know the answer.

Results

Region Channels ROC-AUC AD precision AD recall AD F1
device-like 9 0.815 0.771 0.750 0.761
posterior 7 0.805 0.743 0.722 0.732
whole-head 19 0.790 0.788 0.722 0.754

The device-like subset came out highest. Nine electrodes at the forehead and temples scored 0.815, against 0.790 for all nineteen.

What I am not claiming

Fewer electrodes are not better.

The gap is 0.025. That is inside the 0.05 noise band, which was set before the run. The honest statement is that there is no detectable penalty from dropping to frontal-temporal channels. Not that dropping them helps.

“9 electrodes beat 19” would have been a better headline. It would also have been wrong. Having the threshold written down first is what made that an easy call instead of an argument with myself.

Posterior-only came in at 0.805, also within noise of both. All three land in the same place.

With this sample size and these features, the signal does not appear to be strongly localised anywhere. That is more interesting than the result I was looking for, and I do not fully know what to make of it.

The likely explanation is that my features are coarse. Relative band powers averaged across channels describe the overall shape of the spectrum, and Alzheimer’s slowing is fairly global. The posterior localisation in the literature usually comes from more sensitive methods — source localisation, connectivity measures, event-related paradigms. Four band-power ratios may just be too blunt to see where the signal comes from.

Limitations

Sixty-five subjects is small. Every number here carries wide uncertainty. Treat the table as directional.

The channel subsets approximate the device. They do not replicate it. Clinical wet electrodes at F7 and T3 are not dry contacts pressed against a temple by a plastic frame. Real dry-electrode data will be noisier and this experiment says nothing about how much.

The eye-tracking half of the design is not tested at all. ds004504 is EEG only.

And this is one dataset. A finding that does not replicate is not a finding.

What changed

Electrode placement moved from an open risk to a documented decision. I can say the positioning was tested against the alternative on real clinical data and no penalty was detected. I can also say how confident that is: moderately, on 65 subjects, with coarse features.

I work in AI data quality. My job is finding problems in other people’s datasets before they reach a model. Turning that on my own design was harder, because I wanted a particular answer.

The experiment could have told me the form factor was wrong. That is why it was worth running.

Code: [https://github.com/Bhumii-AI-IoT/alzheimer-ai-device]
The script is channel_region_experiment.py.

If you have worked with dry-electrode EEG or frontal-temporal montages, I would like to know whether this matches your experience — particularly whether the lack of localisation is expected with band-power features, or whether it points to something wrong in my extraction. I am learning this in public and corrections are welcome.
aiSummary: 作者通过将一部分临床 EEG 数据与全头导联进行对比测试，验证了一款已注册的用于阿尔茨海默病检测的 EEG 可穿戴设备的电极放置位置。
oneSentenceSummary: 作者通过将一部分临床 EEG 数据与全头导联进行对比测试，验证了一款已注册的用于阿尔茨海默病检测的 EEG 可穿戴设备的电极放置位置。
summary: 作者描述了对一款用于检测阿尔茨海默病早期迹象的 EEG 头戴式设备所进行的严谨自我验证过程。作者意识到一个潜在缺陷——该设备的前额-颞部放置方式避开了文献中通常认为信号最强的后部区域——于是使用 OpenNeuro ds004504 数据集进行了对比实验。通过将一致的机器学习流程（Welch PSD 和随机森林）应用于“类设备”、“后部”和“全头”通道子集，作者发现有限的电极放置并未带来显著的性能损失。文章强调了科学严谨性：预先设定成功阈值以避免确认偏差，同时承认所使用的粗粒度特征和小样本量存在局限性。

mainPoints.point: 通过数据子集验证设备形态
mainPoints.explanation: 作者测试了将 EEG 传感器仅放置在额头和太阳穴（该设备的设计）是否会相比全头临床设置牺牲诊断准确性。

mainPoints.point: 通过预设阈值减少确认偏差
mainPoints.explanation: 为了避免在看到结果后进行“事后讲故事”，作者在实验前设定了一个噪声阈值（0.05 ROC-AUC），以客观判断结果是否显著。

mainPoints.point: 发现：粗粒度特征下信号定位不强
mainPoints.explanation: 结果表明各区域的表现相似，说明简单的频带功率比可能过于粗糙，无法捕捉阿尔茨海默病典型的局部后部慢波活动。

mainPoints.point: 临床近似与实际硬件之间的区别
mainPoints.explanation: 作者明确指出，使用临床湿电极数据来验证干电极设计是一种近似方法，没有考虑实际硬件增加的噪声。

keyQuotes: 对于一款旨在跟踪数月变化而非捕捉单次临床快照的设备，持续佩戴比任何单次测量的完美信号更重要。
如果先有结果后有阈值，我可能会找到办法把几乎任何结果都解读为验证。
诚实的说法是，缩减到额颞导联并没有可检测到的性能损失，而不是说缩减有助于性能。
